note: Curated list of known open work per bot. The automated static check reads the scripts and cannot see these — they come from live call testing and from features we know are unfinished. Keep this file current; the daily digest reads it verbatim. Remove an item the day it is genuinely closed.

items.title: The "apply for the job" step has never been confirmed working on this bot
items.what: In the last test call the bot tried to submit the application using an internal record number instead of the caller's proper profile ID, and the backend rejected it (404 "invalid or missing profile_id"). The Hindi version of the same bot applies successfully, so this is specific to the Kannada inbound bot — or to the test profile that call used, which had been left in a bad state by an earlier test.
items.why: Applying to a job is the whole point of the call. Until a clean test passes, we cannot say this bot can actually place an application for a Kannada caller who rings in.
items.next: Re-test with a freshly created caller profile and confirm the application goes through. If it fails again, the fix is to read the profile ID the same way the working Hindi bot does.

items.title: The weekly real-phone-call test is not switched on yet
items.what: This daily check only reads the scripts; it never dials a phone. The planned weekly test that places actual calls to each bot cannot run from the cloud yet, because the phone-platform and backend keys it needs have not been added to the GitHub repository secrets.
items.why: Reading a script catches wrong wording and wrong field names, but only a real call catches problems in how the bot actually behaves on the phone — speech recognition, tone, and whether the backend truly saves the data.
items.next: Add the Raya platform token and the backend API keys as GitHub Actions secrets, then enable the weekly live job.

items.title: Two call outcomes are not being captured after the call ends
items.what: Each bot has a separate "output" script that reads the finished conversation and pulls out structured results. Two useful results are not being extracted yet: whether the caller gave consent, and whether they are ready for an interview.
items.why: Without these, the team has to listen to or read the transcript to answer basic questions like "how many callers consented?" — it cannot be reported automatically.
items.next: Add both fields to each agent's output script and confirm they populate on a real call.

items.title: Job list used for testing is not the real production job list
items.what: The job openings these bots read out during testing are sample entries. The real, current openings are maintained by the team directly on the phone-platform console.
items.why: A bot can pass every test and still fail in production if it offers a job whose ID no longer exists — the application then errors out for a real caller.
items.next: Confirm each bot is pointed at the live job list before the next production run, and re-check after the team updates openings.

items.title: Slightly stiff wording when the bot refers to the caller's details
items.what: On outbound calls the bot says "प्रोफाइल" (profile) where the warmer, more everyday "जानकारी" (your details) would sound more natural to a worker.
items.why: Cosmetic only — nothing breaks. It affects how natural the bot sounds, not whether the call succeeds.
items.next: Swap the wording next time these scripts are edited for something else; not worth a dedicated deployment.

items.title: The bot hints out loud that it looked the caller up
items.what: The script explicitly says the caller must never hear that a lookup happened. In test calls on 2026-08-04 the bot said “ನಾನು ನೋಡ್ತಿದ್ದೀನಿ” (“I’m having a look”) on the outbound call, and “ನಿಮ್ಮ ಮಾಹಿತಿಯಲ್ಲಿ … ಕಾಣ್ತಿದೆ” (“I can see in your information”) on the inbound one — both reveal it.
items.why: The prose already forbids this clearly, so it is a model-adherence miss rather than a missing instruction; adding more wording tends to make it worse. Impact is on how natural and discreet the call feels, not on whether it succeeds — nothing fails because of it.
items.next: Try a structural fix rather than more prose: bind the post-fetch turn to a fixed opening phrase so there is no room to narrate. Check the Hindi twins for the same phrasing first — do not change Kannada alone if both drift.

items.title: Two inbound bots could not be driven as far as the apply-confirmation step
items.what: The split-turn confirm fix was deployed to all 12 bots and live-verified on 10. On these two the test call never reached the confirmation step: both said no job in the list matched what the caller asked for, so the conversation ended before the point being tested. That is correct behaviour given the test job list, not a fault.
items.why: The edit is identical to the ten that passed, so it is very likely fine — but the house rule is that a variant is only proven by its own call, never assumed from a twin.
items.next: Re-run with a job list that matches what the inbound flow will actually offer these two bots, and confirm the separate consent question appears.

items.title: The new "can you hear me?" opening turn is live on 9 more bots but has only been tested on one of them
items.what: Outbound bots now open with a short audio check and only give their real introduction after the caller confirms. That behaviour was tested on live calls for KKB Hindi Signals and works there. The same change was then applied to nine more outbound bots and deployed, but none of those nine has had its own test call yet.
items.why: A change that works in one language or on one bot is not proof it works on its twin — the speech recognition, the voice, and the way the model follows the instruction all differ per language. This is exactly the case where assuming would be a mistake.
items.next: Run one live call per bot — Hindi and Kannada, legacy and Signals — and confirm three things in each transcript: the first thing said is only the audio check, the real introduction comes after the caller answers, and a caller who cannot hear gets exactly one slower repeat and then a polite goodbye.

items.title: The new TRRAIN follow-up bot works on the happy path but several scenarios are still untested
items.what: TRRAIN calls seekers who already applied to a job and offers them one free support service. Live calls confirm the Hindi bot handles the ordinary case correctly and handles a missing job title without ever reading "Not Available" aloud. Still untested: what happens when we reach the wrong person (the offer must not be made at all), the Kannada version end to end, and a re-test of the fix that makes the bot name the actual job the person applied to.
items.why: The wrong-person case is the one that matters most for trust — offering a service to somebody who never applied to anything, on a call that opens by telling them they did, is the worst outcome this bot can produce.
items.next: Run the wrong-person scenario on the Hindi bot, run the decline scenario on the Kannada bot, and re-run the ordinary case to confirm the bot now says the real job title instead of a vague "a job".

items.title: Two new features are live on one bot only, on purpose, until they are confirmed
items.what: Two additions are running on KKB Hindi Signals and nowhere else: a line that references a previous conversation when we genuinely have one on record, and a single offer of help from a service provider made just before the call ends. Both were asked to be piloted on one bot before being copied to the rest.
items.why: The first one took two attempts to make work and must be seen firing on a real call before it is copied anywhere. The second one silently did not happen on a call where the caller was undecided, which was fixed but not yet re-confirmed.
items.next: Confirm both on live calls for this bot, then copy them to the other KKB bots and to Maya. Neither belongs on DKB — its caller is the employer, so an offer to help someone find a job makes no sense there.

items.title: On one call out of nine the bot said its introduction twice
items.what: After the new opening turn was added, nine live calls were checked. Eight said the introduction exactly once. On the ninth the bot said it, looked the caller up, and then said the whole introduction again before continuing. On that call the lookup happened earlier than usual, which is probably what pushed it into repeating itself.
items.why: Hearing the same introduction twice makes the bot sound broken, even though the rest of the call was fine. One in nine is too often to ignore and too rare to be the normal behaviour.
items.next: Watch for it across the next batch of calls on any outbound bot. If it recurs, the fix is a rule that the introduction is spoken once per call and never repeated — the same rule that fixed an identical repeat on the new TRRAIN bot.

items.title: The caller lookup was skipped entirely on one call, with no reason visible
items.what: The new TRRAIN bot is meant to look the caller up once, silently, so it can greet them by name. It did so on four live calls and skipped it completely on a fifth — no attempt at all — with the same instruction in place. On that call it also greeted the caller with a name that merely sounded like the one supplied.
items.why: This is the model not following a clear instruction rather than the instruction being unclear, so writing the rule more forcefully tends to make things worse, not better. It matters because a skipped lookup means no name, and a guessed name is worse than none.
items.next: The name problem is fixed — the bot is now told to say the name exactly as given or leave it out entirely. The skipped lookup should be raised with the platform team rather than patched in the script. The bot copes without it: it drops the name and still names the job correctly, because the job title comes from a supplied value.

items.title: The "we spoke last time" opening is built and its blocker is fixed, but it has still never been seen working
items.what: This opening never happened on four test calls. The reason turned out not to be the script at all: the bots had caller-memory switched ON but no memory-writing instructions, so the platform was supplying an always-empty memory and throwing away anything the campaign sent in its place. Proved by running the same test twice on a scratch bot with only that one setting changed — with it off the bot read the memory back word for word, with it on the bot said the memory was empty. The missing memory-writing instructions have now been added to all six KKB bots, so a memory is written after every call from here on. A first attempt at a two-call test (one call to create the memory, a second to use it) still opened the ordinary way, but only about three minutes separated them and there is no way to look at the stored memory to check whether it had been written yet, so that attempt proves nothing either way.
items.why: The feature was one of four requested changes and it is the only one not yet seen working. The blocker is understood and fixed, so what remains is confirmation rather than investigation — and it should not be copied to other bots until it is confirmed.
items.next: Leave the script alone — no more wording changes; four rules were already rewritten chasing this and none of them was the cause. Once a few real calls have gone through and memories have been written, place a second call to a number that has already been called and check whether the opening references the earlier conversation. If it does, copy it to the other KKB bots and to Maya. If it still does not, the next thing to check is whether the memory is actually being stored — which needs the platform team, since there is no way to read it back.

items.title: Six bots have caller memory switched off, and switching it on would discard what their campaigns send
items.what: Caller memory is either the platform's job or the campaign's job, never both. When it is switched on, the platform supplies the caller history itself and ignores whatever the campaign sends in that field. These six bots currently have it switched off and no memory-writing instructions, so they keep no history between calls — but whatever their campaigns put in that field does reach them.
items.why: Switching memory on for these six would make them remember callers between calls, which is the point of the feature. It would also silently start discarding whatever their campaigns are sending in that field today — and on at least one other bot the campaign is actively sending course and dialling information there. Turning it on without checking would quietly break that.
items.next: For each of the six, find out whether its campaign relies on sending caller history. Where it does not, switch memory on AND add that bot's memory-writing instructions at the same time — the platform rejects memory being on without them. Where it does, leave memory off and keep the campaign in charge.
